             RE:     Project No. 58000, Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission
                     Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region

                    Comments of The University of Texas System, on behalf of its 13 institutions

 Dear Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners:

        The University of Texas System on behalf of its 13 institutions, appreciates the opportunity to
 comment on the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (“Commission”) proposed new rule, 16
 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.252 (Large Load Customer Tariffs) and related amendments
 to 16 TAC § 25.192 and 16 TAC § 25.193 in Project No. 58000.

         The University of Texas System, inclusive of its 13 academic and health institutions, which include
 hospitals, (“The University of Texas System”), is one of the largest public university systems in the nation
 and world. In the System’s past experience, it is not unusual for new campus facilities and
 medical/hospital centers to require transmission level service. Those facilities, however, have always been
 and will continue to be investments that serve the public good and the State of Texas for generations.1
 Hospital and university facilities already fund many of the necessary transmission infrastructure facilities
 for large public facilities through contributions in aid of construction. And as large industrial transmission
 users with consistent and predictable loads, they are customers that ultimately pay for any necessary and
 related transmission system upgrades required for their interconnection through their own rates, so there
 is no cost-shifting to other ratepayers.




         1
              In total, the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board currently lists 157 total State of Texas public institutions
that could potentially be impacted by this rulemaking when those institutions construct future large facilities including
universities, community colleges, health-related institutions, technical colleges, and state colleges (list of institutions available
at https://apps.highered.texas.gov/index.cfm?page=8303C0B742D6A6217C4E7EB75A775804AD92F671EEA28FA27DEB32DFB4609513).

              THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT ARLINGTON . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT AUSTIN . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT DALLAS

       THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT EL PASO . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS PERMIAN BASIN . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS RIO GRANDE VALLEY

              THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS SAN ANTONIO . STEPHEN F. AUSTIN STATE UNIVERSITY . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT TYLER

         THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS SOUTHWESTERN MEDICAL CENTER . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS MEDICAL BRANCH AT GALVESTON
        THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS HEALTH SCIENCE CENTER AT HOUSTON . THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS MD ANDERSON CANCER CENTER

        As proposed, the 16 TAC § 25.252 tariff requirements would apply uniformly to any entity that
meets the proposed 75 MW threshold, without regard to the nature of the load, its purpose, or its risk
profile.2 That treatment is a reasonable response to the load growth that the Commission is addressing
for data centers and similar large, flexible, and speculative loads. However, this approach may not align
with the needs of public universities that can also include hospitals, whose expansions are driven by
patient care and enrollment needs rather than by the kind of demand that prompted this rulemaking. A
hospital or university project that, separately or when combined with existing campus load, crosses or
may cross the proposed 75 MW threshold does not present the infrastructure risk this proposed
rulemaking is designed to address.

        One current illustrative example of the unintended affect the proposed rule may have on the
delivery of patient care to Texans, is at The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, (“UT
Southwestern”), an academic medical center and an agency of the State of Texas within The University
of Texas System. UT Southwestern is currently developing a new pediatric campus in partnership with
Children’s Health that will replace the Children’s Medical Center of Dallas. Although the new pediatric
campus project alone is not expected to approach the 75 MW “large load customer” threshold, UT
Southwestern’s existing load, together with future campus development and infrastructure planning, could
possibly approach or meet the 75 MW “large load customer” threshold proposed in the Commission’s
current rulemaking to create 16 TAC § 25.194 in Project No. 58481.3 This project is one example of the
current and future projects that the institutions across The University of Texas System undertake that
would be included in the wording of the proposed rule. Such projects specifically contribute to the care,
safety, health, and education of the Texas community.

       Additionally, §§ 25.252(c)(3) and 25.252(e)(2) of the proposed rule impose a mandatory 20-year
interconnection agreement term and 240 consecutive monthly payments at a fixed minimum billing
demand. It is not clear that these requirements, in application to The University of Texas System, can be
reconciled with Article III, Section 49 of the Texas Constitution, which prohibits the state and its agencies
from creating debt unless the Legislature has appropriated for it.

        The Commission has already recognized a distinction for hospitals elsewhere in its rules. 16 TAC
§ 25.497(a)(1) defines “Critical Load Public Safety Customer” to include hospitals, in recognition of the
fact that electric service to such facilities is crucial to public safety. And the Commission’s own request
for comments in this rulemaking asks whether large computational loads, such as data centers and
cryptocurrency mining facilities, warrant differentiated treatment because of their distinct risk profile. The
University of Texas System respectfully submits that hospitals and public universities do, in fact, warrant
differentiated treatment.

        The University of Texas System therefore proposes the following addition to the definition of
“large load customer” in proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(b)(3):

       (3) Large load customer -- An entity that is subject to § 25.194 of this title (relating to
       Large Load Interconnection Standards), excluding: Critical Load Public Safety Customers
       as defined by § 25.497(a)(1) of this title; and an Institution of Higher Education, as defined
       by § 61.003(8), Texas Education Code, that is an agency of the State of Texas.

        2
            As currently drafted, it is unclear whether there are potential fiscal implications for the state. See Project
No. 58000, Proposal for Publication of Amendments to § 25.192 and § 25.193 and New § 25.252 For Consideration at the
July 9, 2026 Open Meeting at 3-4 (Jul. 9, 2026).
        3
           Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA 37.0561, Project No. 58481,
Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.194 at 9 (Mar. 12, 2026).
  Public Utility Commission of Texas
 August 11, 2026
 Page 3



This addition to proposed 16 TAC § 25.252(b)(3) would exclude hospitals and public safety facilities
under an existing, already-defined category under the Commission’s existing rules and would exclude
public institutions of higher education under an existing statutory definition. The University of Texas
System recognizes that there may also be other ways of capturing the differentiated treatment needed for
hospitals and institutions of higher education within the Commission’s proposed rule and generally
supports the Commission’s consideration of other party comments that propose alternative means of
recognizing differentiated treatment.

     The University of Texas System appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these
comments and is available for Commission questions upon request.

Respectfully submitted,




Jonathan Pruitt
Executive Vice Chancellor and Chief Operating Officer
 Public Utility Commission of Texas
August 11, 2026
Page 4

                       Executive Summary of The University of Texas System

        The University of Texas System, on behalf of its 13 academic and health institutions, which include
hospitals (“The University of Texas System”) files these comments to address one issue in proposed 16
TAC § 25.252 (Large Load Customer Tariffs): as drafted, the rule imposes the same mandatory cash-only
funding, minimum contract term, and minimum billing demand requirements on every large load customer
that crosses the 75 MW threshold proposed under 16 TAC § 25.194, without regard to whether that load
is a data center, a cryptocurrency mining operation, or a hospital or public university campus. As such,
as currently drafted, it is unclear whether or not there are potential fiscal implications for the state.

        An example of the unintended impact the rule as proposed would have is at The University of
Texas Southwestern Medical Center (“UT Southwestern”). UT Southwestern is currently developing a
new pediatric hospital campus that may approach or cross the 75 MW threshold. Unlike the speculative,
flexible loads 16 TAC § 25.252 is designed to address, hospital and university projects are not delayed,
downsized, or abandoned when market conditions shift, and the facilities they serve operate for the
public benefit for decades. It is also not clear that §§ 25.252(c)(3) and 25.252(e)(2) of the proposed
rule, in application to The University of Texas System can be reconciled with Article III, Section 49 of
the Texas Constitution, which prohibits the state and its agencies from creating debt unless the Legislature
has appropriated for it.

        The University of Texas System proposes a narrow addition to the definition of “large load
customer” in § 25.252(b)(3) excluding (1) Critical Load Public Safety Customers, already defined in
§ 25.497(a)(1), and (2) Institutions of Higher Education that are agencies of the State of Texas, as defined
in § 61.003(8), Texas Education Code. However, The University of Texas System remains open to other
mechanisms that achieve the same differentiated treatment.
